title: New Partnerships for Action. Building on the Capital of Environmental Psychology and Architecture
research_question: How can engaging architecture students in live design projects with community groups impact students' intellectual, critical, professional, and social skills, positively affect community groups, and improve society's perception of academic institutions? Additionally, how can interdisciplinary collaboration between architecture and environmental psychology students enrich this learning process and what are its potential long-term strengths and impacts?

participants.description: Students of architecture (University of Strathclyde, UK) and environmental psychology (University of Surrey, UK); community members from Sighthill and Govanhill neighborhoods in Glasgow, UK, including resident associations, youth, language, elderly, sport, and mothers' groups.
participants.recruitment: Local Tenants Association from Sighthill invited the Community Design Unit; Govanhill community contacted the Community Design Unit.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Live design projects in the inner-city neighborhoods of Sighthill and Govanhill, Glasgow, involving students working with various community groups on urban renewal and development strategies.
Participatory design process and interdisciplinary educational program involving architecture and environmental psychology students collaborating with community groups.

measures.construct: Student skill development (intellectual, critical, professional, social, interactive, contractual, presentational)
measures.instrument: Not specified, implied through observation and reflection
Not specified, implied through positive reception and continued engagement

measures.construct: Community capacity building (evaluative, critical skills, confidence, knowledge, planning ability)
measures.instrument: Not specified, implied through observation and reflection

measures.construct: Perception of academic institutions by society
measures.instrument: Not specified, implied through media coverage and professional recognition

measures.construct: Place attachment and sense of belonging in community members
measures.instrument: Not specified, implied through observation and reflection

findings.antecedent: Involving community groups in the design process concerning their city or neighbourhood
findings.consequent: Creation of responsive environments and higher level of satisfaction for communities
findings.mechanism: Community involvement ensures designs are tailored to user needs and preferences, fostering a sense of ownership and pride.
findings.quote: Involving community groups in the design process concerning their city or neighbourhood, can play a constructive role in creating responsive environments and, as a result, achieve a higher level of satisfaction for communities.

findings.antecedent: Engaging students of architecture into live design projects with community groups
findings.consequent: Development of important intellectual, critical, professional and social skills in students
findings.mechanism: Exposure to real-world problems and client interaction provides practical learning experiences.
findings.quote: engaging students of architecture into live design projects with community groups can help develop in students important intellectual, critical, professional and social skills

findings.antecedent: Engaging students of architecture into live design projects with community groups
findings.consequent: Positive impact on the community groups (e.g., services/activities provided)
findings.mechanism: Students' design proposals and engagement provide valuable input and potential solutions for community needs.
findings.quote: have a positive impact on the community groups

findings.antecedent: Engaging students of architecture into live design projects with community groups
findings.consequent: Positive effects on the perception that society has of academic institutions
findings.mechanism: Public engagement and visible community benefits enhance the reputation and relevance of academic work.
findings.quote: it can have positive effects of the perception that society has of academic institutions.

findings.antecedent: Collaboration between students of different disciplines (architecture and environmental psychology)
findings.consequent: Enrichment of the learning process and potential long-term strengths and impacts
findings.mechanism: Interdisciplinary perspectives provide a more comprehensive understanding of problems and solutions.
findings.quote: the collaboration between students of different disciplines can enrich this learning process

findings.antecedent: Sighthill live design project with community groups
findings.consequent: Significant implications on students' academic performance and enthusiasm
findings.mechanism: Real-world engagement and client interaction motivated students and improved their work quality.
findings.quote: The experience had significant implications on students' academic performance and on the enthusiasm of some of the participants involved in the work.

findings.antecedent: Sighthill live design project with community groups
findings.consequent: Positive reception from community groups, university, profession, and media
findings.mechanism: The project delivered valuable outcomes and fostered engagement across various stakeholders.
findings.quote: This project was well received by: the community groups involved... the University... the profession... and finally by the media

findings.antecedent: Govanhill live design project with community groups
findings.consequent: Community groups having access to student work for future plans and potential use for development
findings.mechanism: The design process generated tangible proposals that could inform future community development initiatives.
findings.quote: The client groups from the community have - by the end of this process - available the full range of student work; they organized it in an exhibition and kept it available for future plans. There are chances that this work will be of use to the community

findings.antecedent: Govanhill experience (building on Sighthill lessons)
findings.consequent: Valuable experience for students, community, and academic leaders, reinforcing design and integrating environmental psychology curriculum
findings.mechanism: The project provided practical application of knowledge and fostered interdisciplinary learning and community engagement.
findings.quote: Govanhill has been a valuable experience for the students, the community and the academic leaders that have delivered the course; with no doubt, it has enjoyed the lessons learned in Sighthill, and has established since then regular contacts with the community groups, reinforcing the design aspect of the work, and basing it upon (parts of) the psychology and architecture curriculum.

findings.antecedent: Collaboration between environmental psychology and architecture
findings.consequent: Enhanced attention to the quality of the environment and its implications for people, and encouragement of innovative initiatives
findings.mechanism: Integrating psychological insights into design leads to more human-centered and effective environmental solutions.
findings.quote: achieved successes, such as an enhanced attention to the quality of the environment and its implications for people, and the encouragement of innovative initiatives.

findings.antecedent: Engaging participants in the design and development decision process
findings.consequent: Sense of having contributed, pride for research/design work, and confidence in its foundations (for students)
findings.mechanism: Active participation and ownership in the design process fosters personal and professional pride.
findings.quote: Sense of having contributed to the design and development decision process instilled in participants. Pride for their research/design work; confidence in its foundations

findings.antecedent: Engaging community groups in discussion about their environment
findings.consequent: Pride in having a say, place attachment, sense of belonging, and recognition (for community groups)
findings.mechanism: Direct involvement in shaping their environment fosters a stronger emotional connection and sense of ownership.
findings.quote: Pride in having a say on the discussion about their environment. Place attachment, sense of belonging, recognition

findings.antecedent: Students working with a client, delivering work, and respecting ideas/deadlines
findings.consequent: More interest in taking responsibility on what has been done (for students)
findings.mechanism: Direct accountability to a client fosters a stronger sense of responsibility and ownership over the work.
findings.quote: Students work with a client, must deliver work, respect ideas and deadlines. More interest in taking responsibility on what has been done.

findings.antecedent: Contributing to the creation of environmental changes
findings.consequent: More interest in looking after things after contributing to their creation (for community groups)
findings.mechanism: Personal investment in the creation process leads to a greater sense of stewardship and care for the resulting environment.
findings.quote: More interest in looking after things after contributing to their creation

findings.antecedent: Collaborative work among participants (students and community)
findings.consequent: Participants learn how to be reliable, to ask and offer advice, and share responsibilities
findings.mechanism: Working in a team environment fosters interpersonal skills and mutual support.
findings.quote: Collaborative work: participants learn how to be reliable, to ask and offer advice.

findings.antecedent: Collaborative work among participants (students and community)
findings.consequent: Development of trust and establishment of links/connections within the area
findings.mechanism: Shared goals and joint efforts build rapport and strengthen community ties.
findings.quote: Development of trust and establishment of links/connections within the area

findings.antecedent: Students contributing technical knowledge, enthusiasm, and time to design proposals
findings.consequent: Design proposals having a strong degree of sustainability
findings.mechanism: Student input, especially when guided by interdisciplinary knowledge, can lead to more robust and sustainable design solutions.
findings.quote: Students contribute with technical knowledge, enthusiasm and time. The design proposals suggested have a good chance to hold a strong degree of sustainability.

findings.antecedent: Community groups acting as experts of their area and receiving 'free' contribution from technical experts (students)
findings.consequent: Outcomes that are more responsive to the context, users, local resources, and building capacity
findings.mechanism: Combining local knowledge with technical expertise ensures designs are highly relevant and feasible.
findings.quote: Community groups are the experts of their area, and can enjoy the 'free' contribution from technical experts. Outcomes are more responsive to a) the context; b) the users; c) the local resources and building capacity

findings.antecedent: Engaging students in live design projects
findings.consequent: Development of interactive, contractual, presentational, social, and intellectual skills (for students)
findings.mechanism: Real-world project demands and client interactions necessitate the development of a broad range of practical skills.
findings.quote: Development of interactive, contractual, presentational, social and intellectual skills.

findings.antecedent: Engaging community groups in live design projects
findings.consequent: Development of evaluative and critical skills, confidence in discussion, and in-depth, comprehensive knowledge of their area (for community groups)
findings.mechanism: Active participation in design discussions and problem-solving enhances critical thinking and understanding of local issues.
findings.quote: Community groups develop evaluative and critical skills, confidence in discussion and 'gain' in-depth, comprehensive knowledge of their area.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to original ideas and valuable scenarios (for community groups)
findings.consequent: Informal training on environmental issues, widened horizons, and mature debating/questioning attitudes
findings.mechanism: Engagement with diverse perspectives and design possibilities broadens community members' understanding and critical engagement with their environment.
findings.quote: They are exposed to original ideas and they are left with a range of valuable scenarios for development. Various groups in the community... receive informal training on environmental issues; their horizons are widened and mature debating and questioning attitudes.

findings.antecedent: Unclear goals and unrealistic scenarios in collaborative/participatory projects
findings.consequent: Risk to raise expectations in participants
findings.mechanism: Lack of clear communication about achievable outcomes can lead to disappointment and frustration.
findings.quote: Risk to raise expectations in participants: goals and realistic scenarios of what can be achieved must be clearly stated immediately.

findings.antecedent: Students' projects rarely delivering concrete and finite outcomes
findings.consequent: Clients must be aware that outcomes are a repertoire of ideas, not final products
findings.mechanism: Managing expectations about the nature of student work is crucial for client satisfaction.
findings.quote: Students project very rarely can deliver concrete and finite outcomes. Academic priorities must be clear; clients must be aware that what they can obtain from this experience is - for the moment - simply a repertoire of ideas.

findings.antecedent: Unequal willingness or capability to contribute among participants
findings.consequent: Not everyone will contribute to the process with equal skills
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in motivation and ability are inherent in group projects.
findings.quote: Not everyone will be willing - or capable - to contribute to the process with equal skills.

findings.antecedent: Lack of defined roles, competencies, and levels of commitment within the team
findings.consequent: Difficulty in managing the collaborative process effectively
findings.mechanism: Clear structure is essential for efficient teamwork and avoiding conflicts.
findings.quote: It is important to define roles, competencies and levels of commitment within the team.

findings.antecedent: Community group lacking an organization structure
findings.consequent: Increased time spent identifying potential community leaders and target groups
findings.mechanism: An established structure facilitates initial engagement and project setup.
findings.quote: The community group identified should have an organisation structure. During the process, new relationships and groups can - and almost surely will - be formed, but an initial central core helps and prevents from spending vast amount of time in identifying potential community leaders, locating target groups etc.

findings.antecedent: Having an initial central core in community engagement
findings.consequent: Saves time management and helps organizing meetings, but risks being less open to students' contribution
findings.mechanism: A core group can streamline operations but might inadvertently limit broader participation.
findings.quote: Saves time management and helps organising meetings; but risks being less open to students' contribution.

findings.antecedent: Existing grass-root groups in the community
findings.consequent: Can be reinforced, and new ones can be formed
findings.mechanism: Collaborative projects can empower existing community organizations and catalyze new ones.
findings.quote: Existing grass-root groups can be reinforced; new ones can be formed.

findings.antecedent: Local networking and group engagement
findings.consequent: Can reinforce local networking and link the neighbourhood/group to other resources/organisations
findings.mechanism: Collaborative projects serve as a platform for connecting community groups with broader support networks.
findings.quote: Can reinforce the local networking and link the neighbourhood/group to other resources/organisations.

findings.antecedent: Users' requirements and goals not coinciding with academic requirements and goals
findings.consequent: Professionalism and quality of the outcomes must not be affected
findings.mechanism: A balance must be struck to ensure both academic rigor and community relevance are maintained.
findings.quote: Both parts should be made aware of this at the beginning of the process; this should work as a selection criteria for the community group that is willing to open up to a student group. Professionalism and quality of the outcomes instead must not be affected by this.

findings.antecedent: Users' requirements and goals not coinciding with academic requirements and goals
findings.consequent: Students and user groups work in a very realistic environment and the nature of the issues, problems and goals faced must be treated in consequence
findings.mechanism: Discrepancies between academic and user goals force a more pragmatic and context-aware approach to design.
findings.quote: Students and user groups will work in a very realistic environment and the nature of the issues, problems and goals faced must be treated in consequence.

findings.antecedent: Working with large communities and assuming direct involvement
findings.consequent: Not all participants will accept to overcome social, racial, cultural, political barriers and get along well together
findings.mechanism: Social complexities and existing divisions within large communities can hinder full participation and cohesion.
findings.quote: When working with large communities do not assume that those willing to be directly involved will accept to overcome social, racial, cultural, political barriers and get along well together.

findings.antecedent: Addressing work to different groups at the same time, using different tools, in different places
findings.consequent: Need to share results among groups
findings.mechanism: Fragmented engagement requires deliberate efforts to synthesize and disseminate information across all stakeholders.
findings.quote: Accept to address your work to different groups at the same time, using different tools, in different places, but share results among groups.

findings.antecedent: Students being unclear about goals, aims, objectives, or uncomfortable/disrespectful of the client group
findings.consequent: Reduced trust in students to develop right tools, feel responsible, or perceive significant role
findings.mechanism: Professionalism and clear communication are vital for building trust and ensuring effective collaboration with clients.
findings.quote: Students must always be clear about goals, aims and objectives of the process, and be comfortable and respectful of the client group. When this is the case, then trust students to develop the right tools for working with the clients: they must feel responsible and perceive that they are playing a significant role in the process.

findings.antecedent: Adding a 'social' aspect (communal meals) to meetings
findings.consequent: Participants distracted from seriousness, discuss informally, and offer experiences/stories (for community members)
findings.mechanism: Informal settings encourage open communication and sharing of personal experiences, which can be valuable for design insights.
findings.quote: Add to meetings a 'social' aspect: communal meals distract participants from the seriousness that raises when different groups meet. Also, use common and self-prepared meals amongst students: it is very useful to keep them joined throughout the year and is also a moment when work can be discussed more openly. Let community members discuss informally and offer experiences/stories; there is a lot of information and knowledge in them

findings.antecedent: Using common and self-prepared meals amongst students
findings.consequent: Work discussed more openly
findings.mechanism: Informal social interactions among students foster a more relaxed environment for discussing work.
findings.quote: use common and self-prepared meals amongst students: it is very useful to keep them joined throughout the year and is also a moment when work can be discussed more openly.

findings.antecedent: Students from both architecture and environmental psychology developing a stronger confidence in their own discipline thanks to the view that they get of the other one
findings.consequent: Stronger confidence in their own discipline and links amongst groups
findings.mechanism: Interdisciplinary collaboration provides students with a broader perspective, validating and strengthening their understanding of their own field.
findings.quote: Students from both architecture and environmental psychology develop a stronger confidence in their own discipline thanks to the view that they get of the other one. Links amongst groups

findings.antecedent: Engaging students in live design projects (new condition)
findings.consequent: Increased confidence in developing their ideas and design proposals (feeling that these are backed up by a more complete and realistic understanding of conditions)
findings.mechanism: Direct engagement with real-world contexts and interdisciplinary input provides a solid foundation for design decisions, boosting student confidence.
findings.quote: students show increased confidence in developing their ideas and design proposals (feeling that these are backed up by a more complete and realistic understanding of conditions).

findings.antecedent: Traditional studio culture (rarely encouraging specialization, inducing stylistic/personal approaches)
findings.consequent: Students tend to be defensive and patronising when confronted with new conditions
findings.mechanism: A lack of critical engagement and reliance on subjective approaches in traditional education can make students resistant to external feedback or interdisciplinary perspectives.
findings.quote: Traditional studio culture rarely encourages students to specialise on issues; rather, it often induces them to base design choices on stylistic and personal approaches which become hardly justifiable when their experience and scholastic culture is just starting. As a result, even in these changed circumstances, students tend to be defensive and patronising.

mechanisms: Exposure to real-world problems and client interaction provides practical learning experiences for students.
Interdisciplinary perspectives (architecture and environmental psychology) provide a more comprehensive understanding of problems and solutions.
Community involvement ensures designs are tailored to user needs and preferences, fostering a sense of ownership and pride.
Combining local knowledge with technical expertise ensures designs are highly relevant and feasible.
Active participation in design discussions and problem-solving enhances critical thinking and understanding of local issues.
Informal social interactions foster open communication and rapport among participants.
Professionalism and clear communication are vital for building trust and ensuring effective collaboration with clients.
moderators: Age groups (Parr's theory suggests different environmental needs for different age groups)
implementation_implications: Involving community groups in the design process is crucial for creating responsive environments and achieving higher community satisfaction.
Designers should lead efforts to build communities (social, economic, environmental, technological, public policy), but not in isolation.
Professional architectural education should incorporate live design projects with community groups to develop students' intellectual, critical, professional, and social skills.
Collaboration between architecture and environmental psychology students enriches the learning process and leads to more comprehensive design solutions.
Design professionals must cooperate with experts from other fields to reinforce design solutions with diverse knowledge.
Environmental psychology methods (e.g., mental maps, sensory walks, personal construct theory, semantic differential, Post Occupancy Evaluation) should be integrated into the design process.
A structured approach (e.g., Multi Modal Strategy) is needed for the gradual elaboration of design criteria, values, and judgments, with criteria generated first within the community.
Clear roles, competencies, and levels of commitment must be defined within interdisciplinary design teams.
Expectations of participants (students and community) must be managed by clearly stating achievable goals and realistic scenarios.
Social rituals, such as communal meals, can foster informal discussion and knowledge sharing among participants.
Students need to be encouraged to be critical in their responses to community demands, rather than treating them as strict design requirements.
The design process should aim to increase the community's ability to do planning and programming and foster community leaders.

tables.description: Lists risks and challenges related to expectations and skills in collaborative/participatory projects.

tables.description: Lists practical issues and limitations concerning organizations, balance of goals, compromises, respect, social rituals, bonding, and studio culture.

limitations: The interpretation of clients' needs/wants is complex and requires preparation to prevent gross assumptions.

When only confronted with students' ideas, residents' demands often ended up being treated as strict design requirements, compromising the overall quality of the design outcomes; students' responses to such demands were not critical enough to elaborate from them.
There is a risk to raise expectations in participants if goals and realistic scenarios of what can be achieved are not clearly stated immediately.
Students' projects very rarely can deliver concrete and finite outcomes, meaning clients must be aware that the output is primarily a repertoire of ideas.
Not everyone will be willing or capable to contribute to the process with equal skills.
It is important to define roles, competencies, and levels of commitment within the team to avoid difficulties.
If the community group lacks an organization structure, significant time may be spent identifying leaders and target groups.
An initial central core in community engagement, while saving time, risks being less open to broader student contribution.
Users' requirements and goals often do not coincide with academic requirements and goals, requiring careful management to maintain professionalism and quality.
When working with large communities, it cannot be assumed that all directly involved participants will overcome social, racial, cultural, and political barriers to get along well.
Students must always be clear about the goals, aims, and objectives of the process, and be comfortable and respectful of the client group to build trust.

Traditional studio culture, which rarely encourages specialization and often induces stylistic/personal approaches, can lead students to be defensive and patronizing in changed, collaborative circumstances.
